title: Of Free Will
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: The Nature of the Will
subpoints: The will determines actions based on understanding and nature
The will is free from external coercion but bound to internal nature
Biblical 'heart' represents the core of human nature

outline.title: Defining Liberty and Ability
subpoints: Liberty is the power to will as one pleases according to character
Ability is the power to change one's subjective state or preferences
Man retains liberty but loses the ability to choose spiritual good after the Fall

outline.title: The Will is Not the Source of Sin
subpoints: The will functions as a mechanism driven by nature
Sin originates from the corrupted nature, not a defective will
External influences do not absolutely compel the will to sin

outline.title: The State of Innocence
subpoints: Man originally had freedom and power to will good
This freedom was mutable, allowing for the possibility of falling

summary:
In this session, Pastor Tito Lyro introduces a 13-part series on the Westminster Confession of Faith, beginning with Chapter 9, 'Of Free Will.' The teaching clarifies the theological definition of free will, distinguishing it from the common secular understanding that man is inherently good. Instead, the sermon posits that the human will is free from external coercion but is necessarily bound to the individual's nature, or 'heart.' This means the will freely chooses what aligns with the person's current disposition, whether that be good or evil.

A key distinction is drawn between 'liberty' and 'ability,' referencing A.A. Hodge's *Outlines of Theology*. Liberty refers to the power to act according to one's character without external force, while ability refers to the capacity to change one's nature or preferences. The sermon argues that while humans retain liberty to choose according to their sinful nature, they have lost the ability to choose spiritual good or to change their own heart without divine intervention.

The session further explains that the will itself is not the source of sin; rather, it is a mechanism driven by the corrupted nature. Using biblical examples, it is shown that actions flow from the heart's condition. The teaching concludes by examining the state of man before the Fall, noting that Adam possessed the freedom and power to do good, but this state was mutable, allowing for the possibility of falling into sin.
